string.text: {=EA_ENG_desc}By 1715, the British colonies in North America were experiencing a period of rapid demographic growth and economic consolidation following the conclusion of Queen Anne's War. Divided into three distinct regions—the farming and maritime-focused New England colonies, the ethnically diverse agricultural Middle colonies, and the plantation-dominated Southern colonies—they were increasingly bound together by the transatlantic slave trade and mercantilist policies. While individual colonies maintained localized assemblies and distinct religious foundations, the expansion of commercial networks and a shared reliance on British manufacturing were subtly binding them to the British Empire. Concurrently, the brutal expansion of the plantation economy, particularly via the escalating importation of enslaved Africans, entrenched deep racial hierarchies that would fundamentally shape the socio-political landscape of the continent for centuries to come.
